items.title: Level 3: Everyday examples of Seeing the Big Picture, Changing and Improving and Decisions
items.body: The easiest way to learn the Behaviours is to link each one to an everyday action. Seeing the Big Picture is shown by someone who knows why their task matters. A clerk who checks an address twice because a wrong letter could delay a payment to a family is seeing the big picture. Changing and Improving is shown by someone who spots a better way and acts on it. A shop worker who notices customers keep asking the same question and puts up a clear sign is changing and improving. Making Effective Decisions is shown by someone who weighs up facts and chooses sensibly. A person who has two job offers, lists the pay, travel time and training of each, and then asks a friend for a view is making an effective decision. In each case the person does something specific. Thinking is not enough, and neither is simply having an opinion. For entry-level roles the assessor wants a small, true story. It does not need to involve a large organisation or a big result. A neighbour who started a rota for bin days, or a student who found a quicker way to share notes, can show these Behaviours as well as a paid employee can. When you read an example, ask: what exactly did this person do, and which Behaviour does that action show?

questions.prompt: A clerk checks an address twice because a wrong letter could delay a family's payment. Which Behaviour does this show?
questions.hint: The clerk understands why the task matters to others, which is Seeing the Big Picture.

questions.prompt: A shop worker notices customers keep asking one question and puts up a clear sign. Which Behaviour is this?
questions.hint: Spotting a problem and acting to fix it shows Changing and Improving.

questions.prompt: A person lists the pay, travel time and training of two job offers and then asks a friend for a view. Which Behaviour is this?
questions.hint: Weighing facts and seeking advice is Making Effective Decisions.

questions.prompt: A neighbour starts a rota for bin days so nobody forgets. Which Behaviour does this show best?
questions.hint: Introducing a better way of doing a regular task is Changing and Improving.

questions.prompt: A student finds a quicker way for the class to share notes and shows everyone. Which Behaviour is this?
questions.hint: Suggesting and sharing an improvement is the core of this Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which of these is thinking only, not yet a Behaviour in action?

options.text: Believing that a better filing system might exist
Showing a new starter how to find a folder
Setting up a new filing system with a label for each folder
Asking colleagues to try the new filing system

questions.hint: Behaviours are shown by what you do, and believing something is not an action.

questions.prompt: A call handler tells a caller why a form must be signed, because it protects the caller's own benefit. Which Behaviour is closest?
questions.hint: Explaining how a rule serves the wider purpose links to Seeing the Big Picture.

questions.prompt: Someone is choosing between two evening courses and compares cost, length and whether a certificate is given. Which Behaviour is closest?
questions.hint: Comparing options on clear criteria shows effective decision-making.

questions.prompt: What does an assessor mainly want from an entry-level example?

options.text: A large project that had a major result for the department
A copy of every certificate you have gained so far
A list of the skills you believe you have developed
A small, true story that shows what you did

questions.hint: Small, true and specific stories work well at entry level.

questions.prompt: How large does an organisation need to be for an example to be valid?

options.text: It must come from a company employing over 100 staff
It must come from a government office or public body
It can come from anywhere, including a street or a class
It must come from a paid job based in an office

questions.hint: Good examples can come from any setting where you took action.

items.title: Level 3: Everyday examples of Leadership, Communicating and Working Together
items.body: Here are more everyday actions linked to Behaviours. Leadership at entry level might be a person who, when a new volunteer arrives and looks lost, welcomes them, explains the routine and checks they are comfortable. Nobody asked them to do it. They saw it was needed and set a good example. Communicating and Influencing might be a person who writes a short, clear message to parents about a change of date, using plain words and checking that every family has received it. It could also be someone who calmly explains to an upset customer what can and cannot be done. Working Together might be a person who, when a team is short-staffed, offers to take on an extra task and later asks a colleague for help in return. It also includes making sure everyone is heard at a meeting. You can often tell these three apart by asking what the person was mainly trying to achieve. If the aim was to set a positive example and support others, think Leadership. If the aim was to get a message across or change someone's mind with reasons, think Communicating and Influencing. If the aim was to make the group work well together, think Working Together. Most good stories show some of each, but one will stand out.

questions.prompt: A volunteer welcomes a lost-looking newcomer, explains the routine and checks they are comfortable. Which Behaviour is this?
questions.hint: Setting a welcoming example and supporting others is entry-level Leadership.

questions.prompt: A person writes a short clear message to parents about a date change and checks every family got it. Which Behaviour is this?
questions.hint: A clear message, checked for understanding, is Communicating and Influencing.

questions.prompt: A person calmly explains to an upset customer what can and cannot be done. Which Behaviour is closest?
questions.hint: Explaining calmly and clearly to an upset person is communicating.

questions.prompt: During a staff shortage, a person offers to take on an extra task and later asks a colleague for help in return. Which Behaviour is this?
questions.hint: Sharing the load and helping each other is Working Together.

questions.prompt: A person at a meeting makes sure that quieter members are asked for their view. Which Behaviour is closest?
questions.hint: Making sure everyone is heard supports teamwork and inclusion.

questions.prompt: What question helps you tell Leadership, Communicating and Working Together apart?

options.text: How many people were involved in the story in total?
In which type of building did the event take place?
How long did the whole task end up taking to finish?
What was the person mainly trying to achieve?

questions.hint: The main aim of the action points to the Behaviour.

questions.prompt: A person stays calm in a busy week and helps two newer colleagues find the right forms. Which Behaviour stands out?
questions.hint: Calm example and support for newer colleagues is Leadership.

questions.prompt: Someone explains to a group, with reasons, why moving a meeting to Tuesday would suit more people, and the group agrees. Which Behaviour is closest?

options.text: Leadership and setting a good example
Delivering at Pace under time pressure

questions.hint: Persuading with clear reasons is influencing.

questions.prompt: A person uses plain words and a short list to explain a new rule to a neighbour who struggles with English. Which Behaviour is this?
questions.hint: Adapting your language to the listener is a communication skill.

questions.prompt: How many Behaviours do most real stories show?

options.text: They often show several, but one stands out
They show all nine at the same time
They show none until a manager has marked them
They show exactly one and never any other

questions.hint: Real stories overlap, but you should build the answer around one.

items.title: Level 3: Everyday examples of learning, quality and pace
items.body: The last group of Behaviours can also be spotted in everyday life. Developing Self and Others is shown by someone who sees they are weak at something and does something about it. A parent who attends an evening class to learn computer skills so they can help their child with homework is developing themselves. A person who shows a younger cousin how to fill in a job application is developing others. Managing a Quality Service is shown by someone who cares about getting things right for the person relying on them. A volunteer who checks the names on a list twice before a food parcel is handed out is managing a quality service. So is a worker who keeps a log of every enquiry so none is lost. Delivering at Pace is shown by someone who gets things finished on time under pressure. A person who has five jobs to finish before a school run, puts them in order of importance and completes the key ones is delivering at pace. A useful tip is to look for the key word in the story. Learning and teaching suggest Developing Self and Others. Checking, accuracy and care suggest Managing a Quality Service. Deadlines, order and priorities suggest Delivering at Pace. The examples do not have to be dramatic. They have to be true and clear.

questions.prompt: A parent attends an evening class to learn computer skills so they can help with homework. Which Behaviour is this?
questions.hint: Choosing to learn a new skill is developing yourself.

questions.prompt: A person shows a younger cousin how to fill in a job application. Which Behaviour is closest?
questions.hint: Helping someone else to learn is developing others.

questions.prompt: A volunteer checks names on a list twice before each food parcel goes out. Which Behaviour is this?
questions.hint: Checking for accuracy is the core of this Behaviour.

questions.prompt: A worker keeps a log of every enquiry so none is lost. Which Behaviour is closest?
questions.hint: Accurate records protect the service.

questions.prompt: A person lists five jobs before a school run, puts them in order of importance and finishes the key ones. Which Behaviour is this?
questions.hint: Prioritising and finishing on time is Delivering at Pace.

questions.prompt: Which key words in a story point to Managing a Quality Service?
questions.hint: Accuracy and care point to quality.

questions.prompt: Which key words point to Delivering at Pace?

options.text: Welcoming, supporting and setting an example

questions.hint: Time pressure and priorities suggest pace.

questions.prompt: Which key words point to Developing Self and Others?
questions.hint: Learning and passing on skills suggest this Behaviour.

questions.prompt: A person asks a manager for feedback on their reports and changes how they write them. Which Behaviour is closest?
questions.hint: Asking for and using feedback is developing yourself.

questions.prompt: A person completes a large mailing before the post deadline by stuffing the urgent letters first. Which Behaviour is closest?
questions.hint: Prioritising urgent work to meet a deadline is Delivering at Pace.

items.title: Level 3: Spotting the parts of STAR in a sentence
items.body: A STAR answer is made of four kinds of sentence, and it helps to recognise each one. A Situation sentence sets the scene. Examples are 'Last winter I was helping at a community lunch club that served around forty people each week' or 'In my last job the post room was falling behind'. It says where and when. A Task sentence says what you were responsible for. Examples are 'I was asked to take charge of the booking list' or 'I needed to finish the monthly figures by Friday'. It uses words like asked, needed, responsible and aim. An Action sentence says what you did and uses active verbs: 'I rang each member to confirm,' 'I made a spreadsheet,' 'I checked the totals twice.' A Result sentence says what changed because of you: 'Every seat was filled,' 'We finished a day early,' 'I learned to check the numbers sooner.' If you are reading a draft and cannot find a sentence of one kind, that part is missing. A draft with three sentences about the situation and one short sentence about what you did is out of balance. Aim to include at least one clear sentence of each kind, and then add more detail to the Action. This habit works for application forms and for speaking at interview.

questions.prompt: 'Last winter I helped at a lunch club serving about forty people.' Which part of STAR is this?
questions.hint: It sets the scene with where and when.

questions.prompt: 'I was asked to take charge of the booking list.' Which part of STAR is this?
questions.hint: It states what the person was responsible for.

questions.prompt: 'I rang each member to confirm their place.' Which part of STAR is this?
questions.hint: It says what the person did, using an active verb.

questions.prompt: 'Every seat was filled and nobody was turned away.' Which part of STAR is this?
questions.hint: It says what changed because of the person's work.

questions.prompt: 'In my last job the post room was falling behind.' Which part of STAR is this?
questions.hint: It sets the scene.

questions.prompt: 'I needed to finish the monthly figures by Friday.' Which part of STAR is this?
questions.hint: It states the aim and the deadline.

questions.prompt: 'I learned to check the numbers sooner next time.' Which part of STAR is this?
questions.hint: What you learned belongs in the Result.

questions.prompt: Which words often show a Task sentence?
questions.hint: Task sentences speak of what you were asked or needed to do.

questions.prompt: A draft has three sentences of scene-setting and one short sentence about what the person did. What is the problem?

options.text: It is too specific about the details given
It is out of balance, with too little Action
It has far too many sentences about the results
It uses the word I a great deal too often

questions.hint: The Action should be the largest part.

questions.prompt: If a draft has no sentence about what changed, which part is missing?
questions.hint: Without a Result the story has no ending.

items.title: Level 3: Strengths and Behaviours questions in everyday terms
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Interview questions fall into two broad kinds, and the way you answer each is different. A Behaviours question starts with a phrase such as 'Tell us about a time when', 'Give an example of' or 'Describe a situation where'. It asks for a true story from your past. You answer using STAR, with a clear Situation, Task, Action and Result. A strengths question is usually shorter and about you. It might be 'What do you enjoy most about your day?', 'Are you more of a planner or a go-with-the-flow person?' or 'What makes a good day at work?' You answer in a natural, honest way, in a sentence or two, and you do not need a past example. The panel is listening for energy. A person who lights up when talking about helping people may be a good fit for a customer-facing role. A person who clearly enjoys sorting out records may be a good fit for an admin role. It is fine to say what you do not enjoy, if you say it honestly and politely. Some people try to give a clever answer, but this usually backfires, since the next question is often quick and tests whether your answers are consistent. To practise, write down five things you enjoy doing and five things that drain you, in work and outside. Then think about where the role fits those lists.

questions.prompt: 'Tell us about a time when you helped a customer.' What kind of question is this?
questions.hint: 'Tell us about a time' asks for a past example.

questions.prompt: 'Are you more of a planner or a go-with-the-flow person?' What kind of question is this?
questions.hint: It asks about natural preference, not a past example.

questions.prompt: 'What makes a good day at work for you?' What kind of question is this?
questions.hint: It asks about energy and enjoyment.

questions.prompt: 'Describe a situation where you had to meet a tight deadline.' How should you answer?

options.text: With a short natural reply and no example
With a question back to the panel

questions.hint: Behaviours questions need a structured past example.

questions.prompt: How should you answer 'What do you enjoy most about your day?'

options.text: By asking the panel what they would like to hear
By reading carefully from prepared notes
With a long and detailed STAR story from the past
Honestly, in a sentence or two

questions.hint: Strengths answers are short and natural.

questions.prompt: What is a panel listening for in a strengths answer?
questions.hint: Panels listen for what gives you energy.

questions.prompt: Why can a clever or rehearsed strengths answer backfire?

options.text: It tends to include too many numbers and dates
The panel cannot score answers that were rehearsed
A quick follow-up question may show it was not genuine
It will nearly always take up far too much time

questions.hint: Quick follow-ups test whether answers are consistent.

questions.prompt: How should you handle a question about what you do not enjoy?

options.text: Offer to put the answer in writing instead
Claim that you enjoy absolutely everything
Say you will answer after the interview

questions.hint: Honest answers are fine if put politely.

questions.prompt: Which activity helps you practise for strengths questions?

options.text: Writing lists of what you enjoy and what drains you
Memorising a polished STAR story for each Behaviour
Learning the wording of the job advert by heart
Reading the Civil Service Code aloud several times

questions.hint: Knowing yourself is the best preparation.

questions.prompt: A person who lights up talking about helping people may suit which type of role?

options.text: A role that needs a degree
A role with no contact with others
A role that needs a professional qualification

questions.hint: Energy for helping suggests a good fit for dealing with the public.

items.title: Level 3: Ability tests in everyday situations
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: The Ability tests used in Civil Service recruitment are short and based on everyday tasks. A verbal reasoning test gives you a short passage of text, such as a paragraph about a new office rule. It then gives you a statement and asks whether the statement is true, false or cannot be said from the passage. You must use only the passage and not what you already know. A numerical reasoning test gives you figures in a table or chart, such as the number of enquiries each day in a week, and asks questions such as the total, the difference or a percentage. You may be allowed a calculator, and the instructions will say. A judgement test describes a work situation, for example a colleague who keeps arriving late, and gives you several possible responses. You are asked to choose the best and sometimes the worst. The best response usually fits the Civil Service values of honesty, integrity, objectivity and impartiality, and shows good sense and teamwork. All the tests have a time limit, so it is better to answer every question than to spend too long on one. Practice papers are available. They help you learn the layout and see how quickly you need to work. You do not need to feel nervous about the tests, because most of the questions are about everyday common sense.

questions.prompt: In a verbal reasoning test, what source should you use to decide if a statement is true?

options.text: Only the passage you have been given
What you already know about the subject

questions.hint: You must use only the information in the passage.

questions.prompt: Which kind of test gives you a table of enquiries per day and asks for a total?

options.text: A verbal reasoning test with a short passage
A judgement test about a work situation
A typing test with a short timed passage

questions.hint: Working with figures in tables is numerical reasoning.

questions.prompt: Which kind of test describes a colleague who keeps arriving late and asks for the best response?
questions.hint: Choosing the best action in a work situation is a judgement test.

questions.prompt: What is a sensible approach if you cannot answer a question quickly?

options.text: Spend all your time on that question
Move on and answer the others

questions.hint: Time is limited, so answer as many as you can.

questions.prompt: Which values should guide your answers in a judgement test?

options.text: Seniority, age and length of time in the job
Speed, price and the profit made on each job
Loyalty to friends and colleagues above all else

questions.hint: These are the Civil Service values.

questions.prompt: What does 'cannot say' mean in a verbal reasoning test?

options.text: The passage does not give enough information
You must skip the question and come back later
The statement is false according to the passage
The question has been written wrongly by mistake

questions.hint: It means the passage neither proves nor disproves the statement.

questions.prompt: Who has to be told if a calculator is allowed in the test?

options.text: The examiner will decide at random

questions.hint: The instructions tell you what is allowed.

questions.prompt: What helps you feel ready for the tests?

options.text: Asking for extra time on the day
Reading the whole Civil Service Code aloud

questions.hint: Practice shows the layout and speed needed.

questions.prompt: What qualification must you hold to be able to take the tests?

options.text: A degree in a related subject

questions.hint: The tests check aptitude, not qualifications.

questions.prompt: A numerical test table lists 40, 55, 35, 50 and 60 enquiries over five days. What is the total?

items.title: Level 3: Which Success Profiles element does this evidence support?
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: When you collect evidence for an application, it helps to know which element each piece supports. Behaviours evidence shows how you act: for example, calmly helping a customer in a queue. Strengths evidence shows what you naturally do well and enjoy: for example, being the person friends ask to organise a trip because you like planning. Ability evidence is shown by test results, and by general capacity to learn quickly, such as picking up a new phone system within a week. Experience evidence shows what you have done and learned: for example, two years of caring for a relative, or a placement in a school office. It may be paid or unpaid. Technical evidence shows a qualification or professional skill, for instance a recognised first aid certificate or an accountancy qualification, where the advert asks for one. One activity can support more than one element. Volunteering at a charity shop gives Experience of working with the public, and it could also be the example you use for the Working Together Behaviour. The aim is not to put each item into only one box, but to make sure each requirement in the advert has something behind it. If the advert asks only for Behaviours and Ability, do not worry about Technical evidence. Concentrate on what you are asked for.

questions.prompt: Calmly helping a customer in a queue is best evidence for which element?

options.text: Experience of some kind in a role

questions.hint: It shows how you act, which is a Behaviour.

questions.prompt: Being the person friends ask to plan a trip because you enjoy planning is best evidence for which element?
questions.hint: It shows what you naturally do well and enjoy.

questions.prompt: Two years of caring for a relative is best evidence for which element?
questions.hint: It shows what you have done and learned, paid or unpaid.

questions.prompt: A recognised first aid certificate is best evidence for which element?
questions.hint: A formal qualification is Technical evidence.

questions.prompt: Picking up a new phone system within a week is best evidence for which element?
questions.hint: Learning quickly shows capacity to learn and do tasks.

questions.prompt: A placement in a school office is best evidence for which element?
questions.hint: A placement is something you have done and learned from.

questions.prompt: How many elements can a single activity give evidence for?

options.text: Only two, and one of them must be Technical
Only one, because each activity fits a single element
Several, as volunteering can show Experience and a Behaviour
None, unless it was a paid job with a title

questions.hint: A single activity can give evidence for several elements.

questions.prompt: Volunteering in a charity shop could be used as an example of which Behaviour?
questions.hint: Working with others in the shop shows cooperation.

questions.prompt: If an advert asks only for Behaviours and Ability, what should you do about Technical?

options.text: Ask the recruiter to let you off applying
Not worry, and concentrate on what is asked
Prepare a long answer on it in case it comes up
Tell the panel at the start that you hold none

questions.hint: Only the listed elements need evidence.

questions.prompt: What is the aim when collecting evidence?

options.text: Collect as many different items as you possibly can
Put each item neatly into one and only one box
Avoid using unpaid activities wherever you can
Make sure each requirement in the advert has something behind it

questions.hint: The aim is coverage of what the advert asks for.

items.title: Level 3: Weak and strong answers compared
items.body: Comparing two answers is a good way to see what assessors want. Imagine the question is 'Give an example of a time you helped a team to reach a goal.' A weak answer might say: 'I am a good team player. At my last job we all worked together and the work always got done on time.' It uses 'we', makes a general claim and gives no detail. A stronger answer might say: 'At the community centre, we had to prepare eighty lunches by noon, but two volunteers called in sick. I was in charge of the sandwich table. I asked the helpers on the soup table whether they could spare someone, wrote a new job list on the whiteboard, and made forty sandwiches myself. We were ready at 11.50 and all eighty lunches went out on time. I learned to ask for help early.' It names the situation, says what the person was responsible for, lists what they did in order and finishes with a clear result and a lesson. Notice the differences. The strong answer has numbers, a time and a place. It says I. It describes actions rather than a personality. It also admits something that could have gone wrong. A good test is to read an answer and ask whether a stranger could picture it. If they cannot, add detail. If it is only a claim about yourself, rewrite it as a story.

questions.prompt: What is the main weakness of 'I am a good team player and the work always got done'?

options.text: It has a precise number that cannot be checked
It uses the word I a great many times
It is a general claim with no detail
It is far too long for an answer to this question

questions.hint: It tells but does not show what the person did.

questions.prompt: Which word in the weak answer hides what the writer personally did?
questions.hint: 'We' does not tell the assessor what the writer did.

questions.prompt: What does the strong answer give about the Situation?

options.text: The name of the manager in charge of the centre
A list of the writer's best personal qualities
The age and job history of the writer
A place and a problem: eighty lunches and two volunteers off sick

questions.hint: It sets the scene with specific details.

questions.prompt: In the strong answer, which sentence is the Task?

options.text: I learned to ask for help early
I was in charge of the sandwich table

questions.hint: It states what the writer was responsible for.

questions.prompt: In the strong answer, which sentence states the Result?

options.text: We were ready at 11.50 and all eighty lunches went out on time
I asked the soup table for a helper
I wrote a new job list on the whiteboard

questions.hint: It says what happened because of the actions.

questions.prompt: Which detail in the strong answer shows honesty about learning?

options.text: I was in charge of the sandwich table
I learned to ask for help early
There were eighty lunches to prepare

questions.hint: Reflecting on a lesson shows learning.

questions.prompt: What is a good test of whether an answer is detailed enough?

options.text: Whether a stranger could picture it
Whether it uses plenty of long and formal words
Whether it avoids numbers and dates altogether
Whether it runs to more than a full page

questions.hint: A stranger should be able to see what happened.

questions.prompt: If an answer is only a claim about yourself, what should you do?

options.text: Rewrite it as a story with actions
Add more adjectives to describe your qualities
Make it shorter and more modest in tone
Delete the Result so that it sounds humble

questions.hint: Stories with actions are more convincing than claims.

questions.prompt: What did the writer do in the strong answer to cope with the staff shortage?

options.text: Cancelled part of the event and told guests to wait
Went to find extra volunteers from the street
Waited for a manager to give instructions
Asked another table for help and made a new job list

questions.hint: These are the actions described.

questions.prompt: Which feature makes the strong answer credible?

options.text: Numbers, a time and a place

questions.hint: Specific details make an answer credible.

items.title: Level 3: Fixing 'we' and other common slips
items.body: Many weak answers can be improved with small changes. The most common slip is saying 'we' when you mean 'I'. If you write 'We organised a coffee morning', the assessor cannot tell whether you led it, helped, or simply attended. Fix it by saying what you did: 'I made a list of helpers, I bought the supplies and I welcomed guests.' A second slip is using a vague verb such as 'helped', 'was involved' or 'took part'. These tell the reader very little. Replace them with verbs that show action, such as 'I arranged', 'I wrote', 'I checked' or 'I explained'. A third slip is leaving out the number. 'I raised money' is vague, but 'I raised £320' is clear. A fourth slip is leaving out the Result, so the story just stops. A fifth slip is telling the story in the wrong order and jumping about. Use STAR in order so the reader can follow. A sixth is describing a group's success without separating your own contribution. Say 'my part was'. A seventh is writing a general opinion instead of an example, such as 'I believe communication is important'. Assessors cannot score a belief. They score what you did. Before you submit, read your answer and look for each of these seven slips. Fixing them can lift a weak answer a long way.

questions.prompt: What is the most common slip in weak answers?

options.text: Saying we when you mean I

questions.hint: 'We' hides your own contribution.

questions.prompt: How could you fix 'We organised a coffee morning'?

options.text: It was a great success for everyone who came
I made a list of helpers, bought the supplies and welcomed guests
Everyone who took part enjoyed it very much
The coffee morning was organised by the group

questions.hint: Replacing we with what you did shows your part.

questions.prompt: Which verb is the vaguest?
questions.hint: 'Took part' says little about what you did.

questions.prompt: Which verb shows action most clearly?
questions.hint: 'Explained' names a specific action.

questions.prompt: Which is the better sentence?

options.text: I raised £320 at the coffee morning
Money was raised at the coffee morning
I raised money at the coffee morning

questions.hint: It includes a specific number.

questions.prompt: What happens if you leave out the Result?

options.text: The story stops without showing the effect
The assessor adds one from their own idea
The answer becomes clearer and easier to follow
The form is automatically rejected by the system

questions.hint: Without a Result the assessor cannot see what you achieved.

questions.prompt: Why should you keep STAR in order?

options.text: So that you can avoid using numbers
So that you can use a smaller number of verbs
So that the answer can come out a bit longer
So the reader can follow the story

questions.hint: A clear order is easier to follow and score.

questions.prompt: How can you show your own part in a group success?

options.text: Avoid mentioning the group in the answer
Say 'my part was' and describe it
Describe what each of the others did instead
Keep using the word we throughout

questions.hint: Separate your own contribution from the group's.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I believe communication is important' weak?

options.text: It is much too long for an application
It is an opinion, not an example
It includes a number that cannot be verified
It is written in the past tense by mistake

questions.hint: Assessors score what you did, not what you believe.

questions.prompt: What is a good final step before you submit?

options.text: Copy wording from a stronger application
Read the answer and look for each common slip
Add more adjectives to make it livelier
Cut the Result to stay within the word limit

questions.hint: Checking against the list of slips raises quality.

items.title: Level 3: Turning an advert into a preparation list
items.body: Imagine an advert for an Administrative Officer says it will assess three Behaviours: Communicating and Influencing, Working Together and Delivering at Pace. It also says there will be an online test for Ability and a short Strengths section at interview. The advert gives you a clear plan. First, for each of the three Behaviours, prepare a STAR example. Pick two stories for each so that you have a back-up in case one is not right for a question. Write each one down. Second, practise for the online test using sample papers, so that you know what a verbal reasoning, numerical reasoning or judgement test looks like. Third, for the Strengths part, spend time thinking about what you enjoy and are good at, in work and outside. Do not write a script. Fourth, check any dates and the time and place of the interview, and ask for a reasonable adjustment well in advance if you need one. Fifth, read the role description so that you understand the daily tasks. Sixth, make sure your examples match the grade. An entry-level Behaviours example about listening to a customer is a better match than an example about running a department. Keep a note of the advert's reference number, because you may need it in correspondence. If you are called to interview, take photo ID and any documents the invitation asks for.

questions.prompt: An advert lists Communicating and Influencing, Working Together and Delivering at Pace. What should you prepare for each?
questions.hint: Behaviours are assessed with STAR examples.

questions.prompt: Why prepare two stories for each Behaviour?

options.text: Because the advert states that two are required
So that you can use both in one single answer
So you have a back-up if one does not fit the question
So that the form looks fuller and more complete

questions.hint: A spare example helps if the first does not fit.

questions.prompt: How should you prepare for the online Ability test?

options.text: Ask for extra time on the day

questions.hint: Sample papers show the format and speed needed.

questions.prompt: How should you prepare for the Strengths section?

options.text: Leave it, since it cannot be prepared for
Write and learn a full script for every question
Prepare a full STAR example for each question
Think about what you enjoy and are good at, without a script

questions.hint: Strengths answers should be natural.

questions.prompt: Why read the role description?
questions.hint: It helps you see what the job involves.

questions.prompt: Which example better matches an entry-level Behaviour?

options.text: Running a large department budget for a year
Listening carefully to a customer and solving their problem
Setting national policy for a government team
Directing the work of a team of fifty staff

questions.hint: The example should match the grade.

questions.prompt: When should you ask for a reasonable adjustment?

options.text: On the day of the test

questions.hint: Early notice allows time to arrange support.

questions.prompt: Why keep the advert's reference number?

options.text: It is the pay band for the job
You may need it in correspondence
It shows your score in the online test
It tells you the time of your interview

questions.hint: The number identifies the vacancy.

questions.prompt: What should you take to an interview if the invitation says so?

options.text: A copy of the question paper to follow
A letter from your doctor about your health
Photo ID and the documents requested
A list of the other job offers you hold

questions.hint: Follow the invitation's instructions.

questions.prompt: What should you do first on seeing three Behaviours in an advert?

options.text: Choose one single story to cover all three
Memorise the official wording of each Behaviour
Pick two stories for each and write them down
Wait until the interview to think of examples

questions.hint: Preparing evidence for each listed Behaviour is the first step.

items.title: Level 3: Describing home and volunteer work in work language
items.source: Civil Service Success Profiles framework, GOV.UK
items.body: Learning to describe unpaid work well is a skill in itself. Compare two descriptions of the same activity. The first says: 'I just look after my mum and do the shopping.' The second says: 'For the past two years I have been the main carer for my mother, who has limited mobility. I plan her weekly medicines, book and attend her hospital appointments, manage her benefits paperwork and do the household shopping within a budget of £60 a week.' The second version says what the person does, how often, for how long, and with what responsibility. It uses the same language that a job description would use: plan, book, manage, budget. It does not apologise and it does not boast. Volunteers can do the same. 'I help out at a youth club' becomes 'I run the sign-in desk for forty young people twice a week, keep the attendance register and report concerns to the club leader.' To translate your own tasks, ask four questions: what did I do, for whom, how often or how many, and what was the outcome? Then choose strong verbs and add the numbers. This also helps you decide which Behaviours the activity shows. The carer above shows Managing a Quality Service through accuracy with medicines, Delivering at Pace through juggling appointments, and Communicating through dealings with doctors.

questions.prompt: Which description of caring is better?

options.text: For two years I have been the main carer for my mother and plan her weekly medicines
I do a bit for my mum when I have time
I just look after my mum and do her shopping
I help my mum out in the ways that I can

questions.hint: It says what, for how long and with what responsibility.

questions.prompt: Which four questions help translate a task into work language?

options.text: What did I do, for whom, how often or how many, and what was the outcome?
Who saw me, who thanked me, who helped me and who disagreed?
What was my title, my grade, my pay and my working hours?
Who paid me, where did I work, when did I start and why did I leave?

questions.hint: These questions pull out the details assessors need.

questions.prompt: 'I help out at a youth club' is best improved by adding what?

options.text: The name and background of the club's founder
A list of your other hobbies and interests
An apology that it is only a voluntary role
The number of young people, how often, and your role

questions.hint: Numbers and responsibilities make it specific.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviour does accuracy with a relative's medicines best show?

options.text: Leadership of a team of carers
Seeing the Big Picture of care

questions.hint: Careful, accurate work is the heart of a quality service.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviour does juggling hospital appointments, shopping and paperwork best show?
questions.hint: Managing competing tasks and times shows delivering at pace.

questions.prompt: Which Behaviour does dealing with doctors and speaking up for a relative best show?

options.text: Changing and Improving the way care works

questions.hint: Speaking clearly on behalf of someone is communicating and influencing.

questions.prompt: Which verb is best in a description of unpaid work?
questions.hint: 'Managed' shows responsibility.

questions.prompt: How should a description treat the fact that the work was unpaid?

options.text: It should apologise in the opening line
It should apologise briefly near the end
It should apologise, in order to be honest
It should not apologise, because the skills are real

questions.hint: Unpaid work builds real skills and should be described confidently.

questions.prompt: What is the risk of boasting in a description?

options.text: It is likely to break the word limit
It tends to use up too many numbers
It can sound untrue and may fail under follow-up questions
It can make the answer too short to score

questions.hint: Honest, specific facts are safer than boasting.

questions.prompt: The sign-in desk example adds which useful detail?

options.text: The cost of running the club each month
The name of the club's founder
Forty young people twice a week
A list of the writer's hobbies

questions.hint: Quantities make the role clear.

items.title: Level 3: Checking your examples are true and ready
items.body: Before you use an example in an application or interview, check three things: that it is true, that it is yours and that it is ready to be questioned. True means that every detail is accurate. If you write that you raised £320, you should be able to say how. If you do not remember the exact figure, say 'about'. Yours means that the Action section is mainly about what you did and not about what your team or manager did. Ready to be questioned means that you can answer follow-up questions. Interviewers often ask 'Why did you choose that approach?', 'What would you do differently?' or 'How did the other person react?' Practise answering these aloud. If you struggle, choose a different example. It also helps to keep short notes on each example. Write the dates, the names of the people involved and the key numbers. Review them the night before an interview. If you are asked for an example you have not prepared, take a moment to think. It is perfectly acceptable to say 'Let me think for a moment', and a pause looks better than a rushed, unclear answer. If you cannot think of one, you can be honest and say that you have not met that exact situation, and offer the closest thing you have done. Do not make up a story.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for an example to be accurate and honest?

options.text: It was in a paid job

questions.hint: True means accurate and honest.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for an example to be your own?

options.text: It was entirely your own idea from the start
It is the only example you happen to have
It happened in your own home or family
The Action is mainly about what you did

questions.hint: The assessor scores your own actions.

questions.prompt: Which question is a typical follow-up?

options.text: Where did you grow up and go to school?
What is your favourite colour and why?
What salary would you expect in the job?
Why did you choose that approach?

questions.hint: Follow-ups probe your reasons and learning.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you cannot remember an exact figure?

options.text: Say that you cannot answer the question
Say about, and give the nearest figure
Leave out all of the numbers
Make up a figure that sounds right

questions.hint: Honest approximations are fine.

questions.prompt: What should you do if you struggle to answer follow-up questions about an example?

options.text: Ask the panel to skip it
Add more detail that is not true

questions.hint: If you cannot explain it, it is not a good choice.

questions.prompt: What notes are useful to keep on each example?

options.text: A list of hobbies and other interests
Dates, names of people and key numbers
The names of the people on the panel
Your full pay history for the job

questions.hint: These help you recall details under pressure.

questions.prompt: What can you say if asked for an example you have not prepared?

options.text: That has never happened to anyone
Let me think for a moment

questions.hint: A pause is better than a rushed answer.

questions.prompt: What is the honest thing to do if you have never met the exact situation?

options.text: Describe a story that a friend once told you
Make up a story that sounds believable
Say so and offer the closest thing you have done
Refuse to answer that particular question

questions.hint: Honesty and the closest example are best.

questions.prompt: When is it sensible to review your notes?

options.text: After you receive any offer of the job
Only when asked to by the panel
On the closing date for applications

questions.hint: Revising the night before refreshes the details.

questions.prompt: Why should you practise follow-up answers aloud?

options.text: To make the example shorter than before
To learn the names of the panel members
To use up the time you have been given
To check you can explain your example clearly

questions.hint: Saying them aloud shows any weak spots.
